meta.title: Hazardous Materials Labels

questions.questionText: What is one of the main purposes of a hazardous materials label?

options.text: To provide hazard and safety information
To eliminate the need for PPE

What should you do if you find an unlabeled container?

Treat it as potentially hazardous and notify a supervisor

lessons.label-basics: Hazardous materials labels are the first and most immediate source of hazard information at the point of use. Before a worker touches a container, the label communicates what is inside, what hazards are present, and what precautions are required. Multiple labeling systems exist because chemicals appear in different contexts: OSHA GHS labels for workplace containers, DOT labels and placards for transportation, NFPA 704 for storage facilities and emergency responders, HMIS for workplace safety management, and hazardous waste labels for disposal. Understanding which system applies in a given situation and what each communicates is a fundamental skill for anyone who works with or near hazardous materials.
lessons.ghs-labels: OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard (29 CFR 1910.1200) requires all hazardous workplace containers to carry GHS-compliant labels including the product identifier, pictograms, a signal word (Danger or Warning), hazard statements, and precautionary statements. GHS pictograms use black symbols on white diamonds with red borders to communicate hazard categories such as flammability, acute toxicity, corrosivity, and environmental harm. Labels are the starting point for hazard information -- when workers need more detail on first aid, PPE, storage, or spill response, they must consult the Safety Data Sheet. Employers must ensure all three HazCom elements are in place: labels, SDSs, and employee training.
lessons.dot-labels: The Department of Transportation (DOT) requires hazardous materials shipped by road, rail, air, or water to carry diamond-shaped hazard class labels and, on transport vehicles, larger placards. DOT's nine primary hazard classes include: Class 1 (Explosives), Class 2 (Gases), Class 3 (Flammable Liquids), Class 4 (Flammable Solids), Class 5 (Oxidizers), Class 6 (Toxic), Class 7 (Radioactive), Class 8 (Corrosives), and Class 9 (Miscellaneous). UN identification numbers -- four-digit codes on orange panels or placards -- identify the specific substance so emergency responders can look up the material in the Emergency Response Guidebook and take appropriate action. DOT labels apply during transport, not necessarily at fixed workplaces.
lessons.hmis-labels: The Hazardous Materials Identification System (HMIS) is a workplace labeling standard using color-coded numerical ratings: blue for Health, red for Flammability, orange for Physical hazard, and white for Personal Protective Equipment. Ratings run from 0 (minimal hazard) to 4 (severe hazard). The white PPE section uses letter codes (A through K) specifying required protective equipment. An X code in the PPE section means the chemical requires specialized handling beyond standard categories -- workers must consult the SDS or supervisor before proceeding. HMIS labels give workers a quick at-a-glance hazard summary but are not a substitute for reading the SDS when detailed handling information is needed.
lessons.nfpa-labels: The NFPA 704 fire diamond is used on fixed storage facilities, tanks, and buildings to give emergency responders rapid hazard information. The four sections are color-coded: blue (left) for Health, red (top) for Flammability, yellow (right) for Instability/Reactivity, and white (bottom) for Special hazards such as oxidizing properties (OX), water reactivity (W), or asphyxiation (SA). Each colored section is rated 0 (minimal) to 4 (severe). NFPA 704 is primarily a responder tool designed to give firefighters and hazmat teams a quick overview when approaching a facility -- it is not a complete chemical safety guide for day-to-day worker use.
lessons.hazardous-waste: Containers holding hazardous waste must be labeled under RCRA regulations (40 CFR Part 262). A hazardous waste label must be affixed as soon as waste is first added -- not when the container is full -- and must identify the waste, describe the contents, and display the accumulation start date. Waste labels must only appear on actual waste containers; placing them on non-waste containers creates confusion and compliance violations. Proper waste labeling ensures safe storage, prevents incompatible wastes from being mixed, and supports correct disposal. Employees who generate or manage waste are responsible for labeling containers correctly at the time of generation.
lessons.secondary-containers: A secondary container is any container into which a hazardous chemical has been transferred from its original packaging -- spray bottles, squeeze bottles, pails, or jars. Under 29 CFR 1910.1200(f), secondary containers must be labeled with the chemical identity and applicable hazard warnings unless the transferring employee will use all contents immediately during the same shift. The label does not need to meet the full GHS format but must give other workers enough information to recognize the chemical and its hazards. Unlabeled secondary containers are a common cause of accidental misuse -- workers unfamiliar with the contents may handle them without proper precautions.
lessons.damaged-missing-labels: A container with a damaged, missing, or illegible label is a hazard regardless of its contents. Workers cannot make safe decisions about handling, PPE selection, or emergency response without label information. The correct action is to stop work with the container, treat it as potentially hazardous, keep others away if necessary, and report it to a supervisor for proper identification and relabeling. Never attempt to identify contents by smelling, tasting, or guessing. Never relabel a container based on assumptions. Employers are responsible for maintaining legible, intact labels on all workplace containers and for replacing damaged labels promptly.

1.questionText: Which of the following correctly describes a key function of hazardous materials labeling?

options.text: To add visual appeal to chemical storage areas
To provide workers with hazard and safety information at the point of use
To certify that a chemical has been approved for all tasks
To eliminate the need for Safety Data Sheets

2.questionText: True or False: An employer who maintains labels and SDSs but provides no employee training has met all OSHA HazCom requirements.

3.questionText: A worker finds an unlabeled container in a chemical storage area. What is the correct response?

options.text: Inspect and smell it to determine the contents
Use it only for low-hazard tasks
Treat it as potentially hazardous, do not use it, and notify a supervisor
Relabel it based on where it was found in storage

4.questionText: Which regulatory system requires diamond-shaped hazard class labels and numeric placards on vehicles transporting hazardous materials?

5.questionText: A tanker truck is placarded with a Class 8 DOT diamond. What type of hazard does this indicate?

6.questionText: An HMIS label shows a rating of 3 in the blue section. What type of hazard is indicated?

7.questionText: On both HMIS and NFPA labeling systems, a numerical rating of 0 indicates which condition?

options.text: Minimal or no hazard under normal conditions

8.questionText: Which quadrant of the NFPA 704 diamond represents flammability hazard?

9.questionText: True or False: The white section of an NFPA 704 diamond communicates special hazards such as oxidizing properties or water reactivity.

10.questionText: Why must secondary containers be labeled when a chemical is transferred into them?

options.text: Secondary containers used only by emergency responders are exempt
Other workers need to know the contents and hazards before handling the container
Only secondary containers larger than one gallon require labels
Labels are only required if the container will be stored overnight

11.questionText: An HMIS label shows X in the PPE section. What does this mean for the worker?

options.text: No PPE is needed for this chemical
The label was printed incorrectly and should be ignored
Specialized PPE beyond standard categories is required -- consult the SDS or supervisor
The container should be removed from service immediately

12.questionText: True or False: A hazardous waste label must be placed on a container as soon as waste is first added -- not after the container is full.

13.questionText: A worker is about to move a drum with a severely damaged label -- only partial hazard information is readable. What should the worker do?

options.text: Move it carefully since the partial label suggests low danger
Open the drum to verify the contents
Stop, secure the area if needed, and report the damaged label before proceeding
Relabel it based on what can still be read and continue the task

14.questionText: During a chemical spill emergency, a responder sees UN 1203 on a tanker placard. What does this number allow the responder to do?

options.text: Identify the truck driver's certification level
Determine which employees handled the shipment
Identify the specific hazardous material and look up emergency response procedures
Calculate the volume of chemical in the container

15.questionText: A worker checks an HMIS label before handling a chemical but needs more detail on first aid after a skin exposure. Where should the worker look?

options.text: The shipping invoice for the chemical
The NFPA diamond on the storage cabinet
The Safety Data Sheet for that chemical
